articles.title: Belgium sank 23 concrete blocks weighing 22,000 tons each in the North Sea to build the world's first artificial energy island in a €7B project
articles.summary: Europe News: Forty-five kilometres off the Belgian coast, in the middle of the North Sea, humans are creating something that did not naturally exist in the water. .
articles.body: Forty-five kilometres off the Belgian coast, in the middle of the North Sea, humans are creating something that did not naturally exist in the water. It is the world's first artificial energy island the size of eight football fields, being built with 23 giant concrete caissons, each weighing approximately 22,000 tons. While one might assume that the island would house humans or grow a wildlife sanctuary, its purpose is none of these. It is being built to collect all the electricity generated by future Belgian offshore wind farms and send it to the mainland via submarine cables.The project known as Princess Isabel Island is being promoted by the Belgian electricity system operator Elia. It is being built by the TM Edison consortium, formed by the Belgian engineering firms DEME and Jan De Nul. At the end of January 2026, those in charge announced a key milestone: the last caisson had been manufactured and was afloat. And that's when the decisive phase begins.A power sourceEach box measures approximately 58 metres long, 28 metres wide and between 23 and 32 metres high, depending on the configuration of the storm walls. They were manufactured in the port of Vlissingen (Netherlands), on a production line with five stations that allowed work on several units simultaneously. The complete process for a single block takes around 85 days.DEME confirmed in January 2026 that the final caisson was completed and launched, marking the end of the manufacturing phase. Now, the pieces are transferred to the Scaldia terminal for final finishing before their final installation in the sea.The blocks will not be simply launched into the water and sunk. They will be towed partially submerged to the site, where dredges and ships have previously prepared a bedrock foundation. Once in position, they will be filled with sand so they can sink and rest on that base. The first immersion campaign began in April 2025 with two caissons. It ended in October and will resume this spring of 2026, weather permitting. In total, the operation spans two years, with pauses during the winter storm season. The complete installation cycle—from departure from the port to placement and fixation at the final destination—takes about 24 hours.The island is vital for the European electricity system. It is not an end in itself but a distribution hub. Its infrastructure will combine high-voltage alternating current (HVAC) and high-voltage direct current (HVDC), a very uncommon mix at sea and central to the project's classification as the world's first 'energy island'.In practice, it will consolidate the submarine cables for the new wind farms that will occupy the so-called Princess Elizabeth Zone, a 285-square-kilometre strip of land intended to produce up to 3.5 GW of offshore wind energy. This electricity will then be transmitted to land via high-capacity cables.Furthermore, it is planned to connect with future international interconnectors (Nautilus with the United Kingdom and TritonLink with Denmark), which will allow the exchange of electricity between national networks according to demand and renewable production available at any given time.Nature inclusiveThe design is not limited to just being concrete in the middle of the sea. Elia and her partners worked with marine conservation experts under an approach called "nature-inclusive design" something like design integrated with nature. The exterior walls incorporate protrusions for the roosting and breeding of the kittiwake, a species classified as threatened in the North Sea. There are also submerged structures for marine organisms and specific solutions for the European flat oyster. The NID4BirdLIFE program, co-funded by the European Union's LIFE program, will monitor the nests' development for six and a half years using cameras installed in the walls themselves.The economic figures reflect the scale of the effort. In October 2024, the European Investment Bank approved €650 million in financing for Elia Transmission Belgium for the first phase of the project, with a total estimated cost of €1.105 billion. But, the project has been hit by a dramatic increase in costs, which have risen from an original estimate of €650m to €7bn. This surge is primarily due to increases in the cost of electrical equipment and has raised concerns about the project’s viability.According to available data, the bulk of the civil engineering work should be completed by mid-2026. The electrical infrastructure itself will be installed between 2026 and 2030. The island should become operational around 2030, in parallel with the new wind farms and the onshore Ventilus and Boucle du Hainaut projects, which are responsible for delivering electricity to the end consumer.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ola Electric told to refund Rs 1.34 lakh over EV delivery delay; Rs 1 lakh compensation ordered
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Andhra Pradesh has directed Ola Electric to refund Rs 1,34,161 to a customer after finding deficiency in .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Andhra Pradesh has directed Ola Electric to refund Rs 1,34,161 to a customer after finding deficiency in service over the failure to deliver an electric motorcycle for several months despite receiving the full payment. The commission also awarded Rs 90,000 for loss of livelihood, mental agony and inconvenience, besides Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs. The order was passed on August 31, 2026.Why did the customer approach the commission?According to the commission order, the customer booked an Ola Roadster X Plus electric vehicle and paid the full amount of Rs 1,34,161 on October 2, 2025. The vehicle was scheduled to be delivered on October 23, but it was not delivered even after several months.The customer said he repeatedly contacted Ola through emails, customer support and its grievance mechanism, and also approached the National Consumer Helpline. He alleged that despite these complaints, the company did not take effective steps to deliver the vehicle.He also claimed that the vehicle was registered through OTP on December 31, 2025, even though he had not received physical possession. He later received communication about the registration certificate, but the vehicle was still not delivered.The customer told the commission that he was unemployed and had planned to use the vehicle to earn a livelihood through ride-service platforms such as Rapido. He said he had borrowed money at a high rate of interest to arrange the purchase amount and suffered financial hardship because of the delay.He also pointed out that the price of the same model had increased to Rs 2,48,090, causing him further financial loss.Ola opposed the complaint, arguing that the promised delivery date was only indicative and not binding. It said delivery depended on vehicle availability and completion of government and regulatory formalities.What did the commission find about the delayed delivery?The bench comprising President Karanam Kishore Kumar and member S Nazima Kausar noted that there was no dispute that the customer had paid the entire amount and that the transaction had progressed to vehicle preparation and document verification.The commission found that the customer had repeatedly followed up regarding the non-delivery, while Ola failed to provide sufficient documentary evidence explaining why the vehicle could not be delivered for several months.The commission said an estimated delivery date could allow some flexibility, but could not be used to justify an indefinite delay after the consumer had paid the entire amount.“An estimated delivery date may permit reasonable operational flexibility, but it cannot confer an unrestricted right upon the service provider to retain the consumer's entire consideration for several months without either delivering the vehicle or providing a satisfactory explanation for the delay,” the commission held.It further found that Ola had not produced convincing material showing any specific regulatory, manufacturing, transportation or other obstacle that prevented timely delivery.“A general reference to operational issues or governmental formalities cannot justify a delay of several months,” the commission said.The commission also rejected the argument that registration and insurance of the vehicle amounted to delivery, noting that physical possession was the essential purpose of the transaction.“Registration and insurance are distinct from physical delivery and possession, which were the essential purpose of the transaction,” it held.The commission concluded that Ola had committed deficiency in service by receiving the entire consideration but failing to deliver the vehicle within a reasonable period. It directed the company to refund the full Rs 1,34,161 with 12 percent annual interest from October 2, 2025, until payment.The commission also awarded Rs 90,000 towards loss of livelihood, mental agony, inconvenience, harassment and consequential financial prejudice, taking into account the customer's intended use of the vehicle for earning a livelihood and the prolonged delay.Ola was further directed to pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs. The amounts have to be paid within 45 days of receipt of the order.
